opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most underappreciated pieces of the whole AI stack right now. The core problem is pretty simple: if you want an AI that actually works on your behalf — that knows your email, your finances, your health data, your company's internal documents — you have to hand all of that context to a model running on somebody else's hardware. And today the deal is basically, "trust us." You're trusting the cloud provider, you're trusting the model company, you're trusting every engineer who has access to those machines and every log that gets written along the way.

Secure enclaves, or more broadly confidential computing, change that equation. With the newer GPUs — the Hopper and Blackwell generation from NVIDIA — combined with CPU-side technologies like Intel TDX or AMD SEV, you can now run the entire inference pipeline inside a hardware-isolated environment. The data is encrypted in memory, the model weights can be encrypted, and critically, the operator of the machine — even someone with root access — can't see what's happening inside. And then you get remote attestation, which means the hardware itself cryptographically proves to you exactly what code is running before you send it anything. So instead of "trust us," it becomes "verify."

That matters on a few levels. For users, it means you can actually give an AI agent deep access to your life without that data becoming training data or sitting in someone's logs. For enterprises, it unlocks use cases that were basically blocked by compliance — healthcare, finance, legal — where they just could not send data to a third-party API. And interestingly, it also protects the model developers, because if you've spent a lot of money training weights, you can deploy them on infrastructure you don't own without worrying they'll get exfiltrated.

The way we think about it at NEAR is this is a key building block for what we call user-owned AI. If AI is going to become the main interface through which people interact with the world — with money, with information, with services — then it really matters who controls it. If it's a handful of companies who see everything, that's a very centralized power dynamic. Confidential compute lets you decouple the compute provider from the data and from the control. You can have a decentralized network of GPU providers, and the user still keeps sovereignty over their data and their agent.

Now, it's not a silver bullet. You're still trusting the hardware manufacturer to a degree, there have been side-channel attacks historically, and there's a performance overhead, although on the latest GPUs it's gotten quite small — single-digit percent in a lot of cases. So it's part of a layered approach. But practically speaking, it's the thing that makes private, verifiable AI possible at scale today, rather than waiting for something like fully homomorphic encryption to become fast enough, which is still quite far off.

r001.rationale: The response says enclaves can enable enterprise use cases blocked by compliance, but it does not connect them to access-control concerns that lead organizations to build their own AI clusters.

r002.rationale: It says model weights can be encrypted and inference runs in an isolated environment, but does not state that the weights are decrypted only inside the enclave.

r003.rationale: The response describes protection from machine operators and keeping data out of training data and logs, but does not clearly state that users’ data is private from model developers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core problem is that right now, when you use an AI model, you're sending your data to somebody else's computer. And you just have to trust that company—trust that they're not looking at it, not training on it, not getting breached, not changing the model on you without telling you. And the companies themselves are kind of in an awkward position, because the model weights are their most valuable asset, so they can't just hand them to you to run locally either. So you've got this standoff where the user can't verify what's happening to their data, and the provider can't give up control of the model.

Secure enclaves, or confidential computing more broadly, are interesting because they let you break that standoff. The idea is you have hardware—Intel TDX, AMD SEV, Nvidia's confidential computing on the H100s—where the memory is encrypted and even the operator of the machine, the cloud provider, can't look inside. And critically, the hardware produces an attestation, basically a cryptographic proof that says "this exact code, this exact model, is what's running inside this box." So as a user, you can encrypt your prompt to that enclave, know that only that specific verified program can decrypt it, and get a response back, and nobody in the middle—not the cloud, not the model company's employees—ever sees it in the clear.

What I find compelling is that it flips the trust model. Instead of trusting a brand or a terms-of-service document, you're trusting hardware and verifiable code. And you can take that attestation and put it on-chain, so now you have a public, auditable record of what model was actually served to you. That matters a lot for agents, because if an agent is going to hold my keys or move my money, I want to know it's running the model I think it's running and that nobody swapped it out.

Now, I want to be honest about the caveats. You're still trusting the chip manufacturer—Intel, AMD, Nvidia. There have been side-channel attacks on these systems before, and there will be more. There's a performance overhead, though it's gotten pretty small on the GPU side. And attestation is only as good as the code you're attesting—if the model provider ships a program that logs everything and you just verified that program, you've verified that it's spying on you. So you really need the code to be open and reviewable for the whole thing to mean something, which is why I think this pairs naturally with open-source models and open-source serving stacks.

But I'd say it's one of the few approaches where you don't have to choose between a powerful model and actual privacy. Fully local inference is great but limited by your hardware. Fully homomorphic encryption is beautiful in theory but orders of magnitude too slow for large models today. Enclaves are the thing that works right now, and I think it'll become the default expectation—that when I talk to an AI, I can verify what it is and that my data never leaves a boundary I control.

r001.rationale: The response discusses users’ privacy concerns and providers’ control of model weights, but does not connect secure enclaves to organizations’ access-control concerns or their decision to build AI clusters.

r002.rationale: It says enclave memory is encrypted and prompts can be decrypted only by the verified program, but does not state that encrypted model weights are decrypted only inside the enclave.

r003.rationale: It says the cloud and model-company employees never see users’ prompts in cleartext, communicating privacy from the model developer.

astra-6.text:
I think secure enclaves give us a way to separate who runs the computation from who can access the data. You might want to use a model running on somebody else’s infrastructure, but you don’t necessarily want that provider to see everything you’re sending to it. The idea is that your data is decrypted and processed inside an isolated environment, and the operator of the machine can’t just inspect it.

The important piece is attestation: you can verify what code is running in that environment before you send it your data. Then you can start enforcing rules around how the data is used, what can leave the environment, and who receives the result. That’s a stronger foundation for control than simply trusting a provider’s promise.

It’s not a complete solution—you’re still trusting the hardware and you need to design the software carefully. But it gives us a useful building block for AI that can work with private information without requiring users to hand unrestricted access to an infrastructure provider.

r001.rationale: It describes separating the infrastructure operator from access to data, but does not connect enclaves to the access-control concerns motivating organizations to build their own AI clusters.

r002.rationale: It says user data is decrypted and processed inside the enclave, but does not state that encrypted model weights are decrypted only there.

r003.rationale: It says the infrastructure operator cannot inspect user data, but does not identify model developers as the party from whom data is kept private.

sol-6.1.text:
I think secure enclaves give us a way to separate who operates the infrastructure from who can access the data. You could run a model on somebody else’s machine, but have the inputs and the computation protected inside an enclave, so the operator doesn’t automatically get to see your information.

The other important piece is attestation: you can verify what code is running before you send it your data. So you can start to say, “I’m allowing this particular model to use this information for this particular task,” rather than handing everything over to a service and trusting its policies.

That’s not a complete solution by itself. You still have to think about what the model can reveal through its outputs and who controls the keys. But it’s a useful building block for AI where users retain more control over their data.
